case_name: MITUTOYO AMERICA CORPORATION v. Illinois Department of Revenue
title: MITUTOYO AMERICA CORPORATION v. Illinois Department of Revenue (21 TT 133)
text:
ILLINOIS INDEPENDENT
TAX TRIBUNAL
MITUTOYO AMERICA CORPORATION, )
Petitioner, )
)
v. ) 21 TT 133
) Judge Brian F. Barov
ILLINOIS DEPARTMENT )
OF REVENUE, )
Respondent. )
ORDER ON SUMMARY JUDGMENT MOTIONS
The Petitioner, Mitutoyo America Corporation (“Petitioner”), timely filed its
Illinois corporate income tax return for the tax year ending December 31, 2016. The
return was audited by the Illinois Department of Revenue (“Department”), and no
errors were found. After concluding that income attributable to Illinois should have
been attributed to other states, and that this resulted in an overpayment of Illinois
income tax, the Petitioner filed an amended return in which it claimed a tax refund.
The Department disallowed the refund claim on the ground that the amended
return was filed late. According to the Department, the amended return was due on
October 16, 2020, but it was received by the Springfield Payment Center on October
21, 2020, six calendar days and four business days after the limitations period had
expired.
The Petitioner alleged that the amended return was timely filed under
section 1.25 of the Statute on Statutes, 5 ILCS 70/1.25, because it was mailed on
October 15, 2020, the day before the due date. The Department contended that
because there was no mailing envelope and no postmark, the Petitioner’s reliance
on section 1.25 was inapplicable, the Petitioner’s proof of mailing was insufficient,
and the date that the amended return was received is controlling. The parties have
1

filed cross-motions for summary judgment on the issue of the timeliness of filing
and, for the reasons stated below, summary judgment is granted in the Petitioner’s
favor and against the Department.
Background
The Petitioner’s 2016 year-end amended tax return was due to be filed by
Friday, October 16, 2020. Dep’t Mot., Statement of Undisputed Facts ¶ 3. 1 At
that time, due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the State of Illinois was operating under
the Governor’s Executive Orders that encouraged or directed Illinois businesses to
implement remote work, social distancing and face coverings in the workplace.
See, e.g., Executive Order 2020-43 (June 26, 2020), https://www.illinois.gov/
government/executive-orders/executive-order.executive-order-number-
43.2020.html.
In accord with the state and federal governmental pandemic directives and
the Petitioner’s employment policies, the Petitioner’s in-house tax-specialist,
Michelle Brazee (“Brazee”), was working from home the week of October 12-16,
2020. Pet’r Ex. A, Affidavit of Michelle Brazee (“Brazee Affidavit”) at ¶¶ 1-2. On
the morning of October 13, 2020, Brazee was informed by Petitioner’s outside tax
accountants that the 2016 year-end amended return would be finalized and
delivered to Petitioner’s office on October 15, 2020. Brazee Affidavit at ¶ 4. The
decision to file an amended return had been prompted by Petitioner’s
determination that it misattributed income to Illinois that should have been
attributed to other states and, as a result, it overpaid Illinois income tax. Pet’r
Mot. at 1-2; Pet’r Reply at 2 n.1.
On October 15, 2020, Brazee made a trip into the office, as an exception to
the remote work policy, and when the return arrived, she prepared it for signature
1 The background facts and parties’ arguments are cited as follows: Petitioner’s Brief in Support of
Motion for Summary Judgment (“Pet’r Mot.”), its exhibits (“Pet’r Ex. __”); Petitioner’s Reply to the
Department’s Memorandum in Support of Its Motion for Summary Judgment (“Pet’r Reply”); the
Department’s Cross-Motion for Summary Judgment (“Dep’t Mot.”), its exhibits (“Dep’t Ex. __”); and
the Departments’ Response to Petitioner’s Motion for Summary Judgment (“Dep’t Response”).
2

by the appropriate corporate officer. Id. at ¶¶ 3, 5. On that afternoon, she
obtained the proper signature for the return, placed the signed return in an
envelope, sealed it and affixed the correct postage. Id. at ¶¶ 6-7.
According to Brazee, her normal procedure would have been to take the
mailing envelope to the US Post Office, in Aurora Illinois, stand in line and send it
certified mail, retaining the appropriate stamped documentation. Id. at ¶ 8.
However, due to the severity of the COVID-19 pandemic, the reported number of
cases and hospitalizations in the area, and the fact that she was caring for four
children, Brazee testified, that she “deemed it unwise” to enter the post-office. Id.
Instead, she deposited the return, properly addressed and bearing sufficient
postage in a USPS mailbox on the afternoon of Thursday, October 15, 2020. Id.
The Petitioner’s amended return was stamped “Received” by the
Department’s Springfield Payment Center (“payment center”) on Wednesday
October 21, 2020. Dep’t Ex. A., 2016 IL-1120-X, Mitutoyo America Corporation
Amended Corporation Income and Replacement Tax Return. The Department’s
Document Control & Deposit Division Manager at the payment center, Philip
James, averred that the payment center is “a payment window in the lobby of the
Willard Ice Building located in Springfield, Illinois.” Dep’t Ex. D, Affidavit of
Phillip James (“James Affidavit”) at ¶ 3. Further, James stated that the payment
center was open for business and staffed during the COVID-19 pandemic in October
2020. James Affidavit at ¶ 4. Additionally, James attested to the fact that the
payment center was open during the brief time that the Illinois Department of
Revenue was closed to the public due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Id. at ¶ 5.
According to Mike Dixon, a Public Service Administrator with the
Department, in March 2022, he reviewed the Petitioner’s 2016 amended return file
and did not find a mailing envelope in the Department’s file. Dep’t Ex. C, Affidavit
of Mike Dixon at ¶¶ 1-4.
3

Analysis
The parties have filed cross-motions for summary judgment contesting
whether the 2016 amended return was timely filed. Summary judgment is proper
only where “the pleadings, depositions, and admissions on file, together with the
affidavits, if any, show that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and
that the moving party is entitled to a judgment as a matter of law.” Rogers v.
Illinois Department of Revenue, 2017 IL App (1st) 151449, ¶ 30. Where the parties
file cross-motions for summary judgment, they invite the court to decide the case as
a matter of law based on the facts in the record. Shared Imaging, LLC v. Hamer,
2017 IL App (1st) 152817, ¶ 13. Generally, if a party moving for summary
judgment supports the motion with an affidavit or other admissible evidence that
would entitle it to summary judgment, the opposing party must provide
countervailing affidavits or evidence that raises a legitimate fact question. See
Tafoya-Cruz v. Temperance Beer Co., 2020 IL App (1st) 190606, ¶ 68; North
Community Bank v. 17011 S. Polk Ave, LLC, 2015 IL App (1st) 133672, ¶15. “Mere
speculation, conjecture, or guess is insufficient” to avoid summary judgment.
Tafoya-Cruz, 2020 IL App (1st) 190606, at ¶ 68; Sorce v. Naperville Jeep Eagle, Inc.,
309 Ill. App. 3d 313, 329 (2d Dist. 1999).2
There is no dispute that the amended return was timely filed if mailed on or
before its October 16, 2020 due date. The dispute here is over the application of the
statute governing proof of mailing, section 1.25 of the Statute on Statutes, 5 ILCS
70/1.25. Section 1.25 states in pertinent part:
Unless An Act otherwise specifically provides, any writing of any kind
or description required or authorized to be filed with, and any payment
of any kind or description required or authorized to be paid to, the State
or any political subdivision thereof, by the laws of this State:
2 The Department makes a perfunctory argument that summary judgment is improper
here because the Petitioner has not yet filed an answer. See Dep’t Resp. at 3-4. This
contention is rejected. A motion for summary judgment may be made an any time, 735
ILCS 5/2-1005(a), does not first require an answer, see Delaney Electric Co. v. Schiessle, 235
Ill. App. 3d 258, 267 (1st Dist. 1992), and the Department had ample opportunity to
respond to the Petitioner’s summary judgment motion, see id.
4

(1) if transmitted through the United States mail, shall be deemed filed
with or received by the State or political subdivision on the date
shown by the post office cancellation mark stamped upon the
envelope or other wrapper containing it;
(2) if mailed but not received by the State or political subdivision, or if
received but without a cancellation mark or with the cancellation
mark illegible or erroneous, shall be deemed filed with or received by
the State or political subdivision to which it was required or
authorized to be directed on the date it was mailed, but only if the
sender establishes by competent evidence that the writing or
payment was deposited, properly addressed, in the United States
mail on or before the date on which it was required or authorized to
be filed or was due.
* * * *
If a writing or payment is sent by United States registered mail,
certified mail or certificate of mailing, a record authenticated by
the United States Post Office of such registration, certification or
certificate shall be considered competent evidence that the
writing or payment was mailed. The date of registration,
certification or certificate shall be deemed the postmarked date.
5 ILCS 70/1.25
Subsection 1 of section 1.25 clearly creates a presumption of filing on the date
that a mailing is postmarked.3 5 ILCS 70/1.25(1). Subsection 2 of section 1.25
allows competent evidence to prove the date of mailing when a postmark is absent,
illegible, or erroneous. See In re Application of the County Collector, 265 Ill. App. 3d
485, 490 (1st Dist. 1994). The Department takes the position, however, that section
1.25(2) allows other evidence to prove the date of a mailing only when a document is
(1) mailed but not received, (2) received by mail but without a postmark, or (3)
received by mail but with an illegible or erroneous postmark. In this case, neither
of those three options occurred: the amended return was received but no mailing
3 The cancellation mark referenced in section 1.25 is used synonymously with the term
“postmark.” See Wickman v. Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board, 387 Ill. App. 3d 414, 417
(2d Dist. 2008).
5

envelope is in the record. Without the envelope, the Department contends the
Petitioner cannot use other competent evidence to prove the fact and timeliness of
the mailing. Dep’t Mot. at 10-13; Dep’t Response at 4-6.
The flaw the Department’s construction of section 1.25(2) is apparent. Under
the Department’s view a party may prove the fact of timely mailing when a writing
is not received–in which case there is no mailing envelope– but it cannot prove a
timely mailing when it is received, but there is no mailing envelope. That is an
absurd result. Under the Department’s construction of 1.25(2), a government
agency can avoid the statute’s application simply by discarding or destroying the
envelope. This would effectively nullify section 1.25(2) and no regular mailings
could ever be considered timely.
A statute must be construed according to its plain language but not in a
manner that defies common sense or would render it absurd, inoperative or
meaningless. See, e.g., Progressive Universal Insurance Company v. Liberty Mutual
Fire Insurance Company, 215 Ill. 2d 121, 134-35 (2005); Best Buy Stores, L.P. v.
Department of Revenue, 2020 IL App (1st) 191680, ¶ 16. The Department’s
construction of section 1.25(2) does just that; it cannot be the result intended by the
legislature. See, e.g., Progressive Universal Insurance Company, 215 Ill. 2d at 134-
35 (refusing to construe statutory language restricting automobile insurance
coverage in such a way that the insured could easily evade).
Further, the case law does not support the Department’s conclusion that
section 1.25(2) bars the Petitioner from providing proof of mailing without the
envelope. In the most pertinent case cited, the mailing envelope had been destroyed
by the party seeking to prove a timely mailing, yet the court reviewed testimony
and documents before determining whether the mailing was timely. See
Application of County Treasurer & Ex-Officio County Collector of Cook County, 57
Ill. App. 3d 550 (1st Dist. 1978) (“Application of County Treasurer”). Application of
County Treasurer involved an attempt to redeem real property after a tax sale. 57
Ill. App. 3d at 551. The United States Department of Housing and Urban
Development (“HUD”) was the party that sought redemption on behalf of the
6

property’s prior owner after the property had been sold through a tax sale. Id.
HUD transmitted a redemption check to the Cook County Clerk, which was rejected
as untimely, and the check and mailing envelope were returned to HUD but
eventually destroyed by the federal government and the postmark was not
available. Id. at 552, 554.
A hearing was held on whether the mailing was timely. Oral testimony was
introduced as to: (1) HUD’s procedure for preparing and mailing the redemption
check; (2) the local US post office’s mailing handling procedures; and (3) the county
clerk’s procedure for handling incoming mail. Id. at 551-52. Further, a photocopy
of the supposed redemption check was introduced into evidence, but it showed
neither the property’s correct Permanent Real Estate Index Number nor the correct
redemption amount. Id. at 553. HUD also introduced into evidence a photocopy of
the purported mailing envelope’s back, but it did not submit any evidence of the
envelope’s front, which would show the postmark, and HUD admitted that the
original envelope was lost or destroyed. Id. at 554.
The court did not take the position the Department advocates for here and
simply decide that in the absence of an envelope with valid postmark, the proof of a
valid redemption failed under section 1.25. Rather, it considered the oral testimony
of federal and county government officials as to mailing and mail handling
procedures; the fact that the party seeking to prove a timely mailing failed to
preserve the evidence of a timely mailing; and the discrepancy between the property
redemption check and the property it sought to redeem. Id.
The Department focuses on language in the decision stating that absent
evidence of an envelope “it cannot be said that the envelope was ‘received but
without a cancellation mark or with the cancellation mark illegible or erroneous.’
Consequently, the mailing statute was inapplicable.” Id. at 554. Based on this
language, the Department argues that as a matter of law absence of the envelope
forecloses other proof of mailing. Dep’t Mot. at 11. In Application of County
Treasurer, however, unlike here, the party seeking to prove the timely mailing had
the envelope and lost or destroyed it. Thus, the Application of County Treasurer
7

decision can only be read as a burden of proof case, in which the party proposing the
mailing date had the envelope and did not produce it. To read it, as the Department
does, to categorically bar the introduction of proof of mailing when the envelope is
absent, and the government recipient, arguably, last possessed it, places all the risk
of mailing on the mailing party, none on the government, and, again, threatens to
render the statutory mailing provision meaningless.
The Department makes a corresponding argument that if evidence beyond a
postmark is allowable to prove the date of mailing, the only competent evidence
allowed is evidence of registered or certified mail. It bases this argument in the
language of the second paragraph of subsection 1.25(2):
If a writing or payment is sent by United States registered mail, certified
mail or certificate of mailing, a record authenticated by the United
States Post Office of such registration, certification or certificate shall
be considered competent evidence that the writing or payment was
mailed. The date of registration, certification or certificate shall be
deemed the postmarked date.
5 ILCS 70/1.25(2).
This argument fails the plain language test. See Progressive Universal
Insurance Company, 215 Ill. 2d at 134. Section 1.25(2)’s reference to certified and
registered mail obviously applies only when a mailing is made by registered or
certified mail. In that case, a postmark is unnecessary, and certification and
registration documents can substitute for the postmarked envelope. The present
case does not involve registered or certified mail, and the language the Department
cites does not limit the type of evidence that may be considered to prove a timely
mailing.
Finally, before examining the evidence of mailing here, it also necessary to
address the Department’s fallback argument that the proof of mailing must be
shown by Petitioner’s books and records. See Dep’t Motion at 13, Dep’t Response at
6-8. The regulation that the Department cites in support of this argument states:
“[e]very person liable for any tax imposed by the IITA shall keep books and records
sufficient to substantiate all information reported on any income tax, withholding or
8

information return required under the IITA.” 86 Ill. Adm. Code 100.9530(a)(1)
(emphasis added). Proof of mailing is not a line entry reported on an “income tax,
withholding or information return.” Likewise, the case law on which the
Department relies provides that “[t]o overcome the Department’s prima facie case; a
taxpayer must present more than its testimony denying the accuracy of the
assessments but must present sufficient documentary support for its assertions.”
PPG Industries, Inc. v. Department of Revenue, 328 Ill. App. 3d 16, 34 (1st Dist.
2002) (quoting Mel-Park Drugs, Inc. v. Department of Revenue, 218 Ill. App. 3d 203,
217 (1st Dist. 1991) (emphasis added); see also Copilevitz v. Department of Revenue,
41 Ill. 2d 154, 157-58 (1968); A.R. Barnes v. Department of Revenue, 173 Ill. App. 3d
826, 833-34 (1st Dist. 1988). The accuracy of the assessment is not in question in
this case. The Department denied the refund claim solely on the ground that it was
untimely, not on its accuracy. The books and records rule that the Department
invokes does not apply.
The Petitioner thus is not barred from proving a timely mailing by competent
evidence. The evidence shows that on the afternoon of October 15, 2020, after
obtaining the proper signature for the 2016 amended income tax return, Brazee
placed the return in an envelope, sealed it and affixed the correct postage. Id. at ¶¶
6,7. Her normal mailing procedure was to take the mailing envelope to the United
States Post Office in Aurora, Illinois and send it certified mail, retaining the
appropriate stamped documentation. Id. at ¶ 8. However, she averred that due to
the severity of the COVID-19 pandemic and the fact that she was caring for four
children, she was concerned about the risk of standing inside the post office and
thus deposited the return, properly addressed and bearing sufficient postage in a
USPS mailbox on Thursday, October 15, 2020, one date before the return’s due date.
Id.
The amended return was stamped received by the payment center on October
21, 2020, four business days (or six calendar days) later. Dep’t Ex. A. An affidavit
from the Department’s Document Control & Deposit Division Manager stated that
the payment center is “a payment window in the lobby of the Willard Ice Building
9

located in Springfield, Illinois.” Dep’t Ex. D, James Affidavit at ¶ 3. The affiant
also asserted that the Springfield Payment Center was open for business during the
COVID-19 Pandemic and specifically in October 2020. Id. at ¶ 4.
The Department did not, however, provide any evidence of mail handling
procedures at the payment center. The function of the payment window remains a
mystery. Was it used only for walk-in filings or also for mail deliveries? If it was
used for mail delivery, was it the first point of contract or did mail arrive at the
payment center from some other location of the Willard Ice Building? Once mail
was delivered to the payment center had it already been opened or was it first
opened and processed there?
Moreover, while the Department attested to the fact that it reviewed the
Petitioner’s tax file and did not find a mailing envelope, it introduced no evidence
as to the Department’s policy for handling mailing envelopes. Whether mailing
envelopes were routinely retained, photocopied or electronically scanned or
discarded remains an open question.
Brazee’s actions were consistent and credible, given the rapid spread of the
SARS-CoV-2 virus, the severity of COVID-19 pandemic and the state and federal
public health actions attempting to limit the virus’s spread in October 2020, a time
when vaccines were not yet available. Further, the evidence of the mailing date is
reasonable. Brazee testified that the amended return was mailed on the afternoon
of Thursday, October 15, 2020, Brazee Affidavit at 7-8, and was stamped as received
on October 21, 2020, Dep’t Ex. A. Viewed as either delivery within four business
days, or six calendar days, the delivery time is reasonable, see, e.g., Sable v.
Commissioner, TC Memo 1996-535 (4 days); McCurry v. Commissioner, TC Memo
1981-68 (6 days); Beacham v. Commissioner, TC Memo 1996-226 (3 days),
particularly given the mailing delays in October 2021 due to decreased resources
caused by the pandemic and increased volume caused by the high demand for mail-
in ballots during the 2020 election season, see Postal Regulatory Commission,
Annual Compliance Determination Report Fiscal Year 2021 (Mar. 29, 2022),
https://www.prc.gov/docs /121/121270/FY% 202021%20ACD.pdf, at 107-24; United
10

State Postal Service, Fiscal Year 2021 Annual Report to Congress,
https://about.com/what/financials/ annual-reports/fy2021.pdf, at 32-35.
By contrast, the Department’s evidence that the amended return could not
have been timely is speculative. Summary judgment is the moment for a party to
come forward with the evidence to support its case. Tafoya-Cruz, 2020 IL App (1st)
190606, ¶ 6; North Community Bank, 2015 IL App (1st) 133672, ¶15. The
Department has failed to provide facts that dispute the Petitioner’s evidence of
timely mailing.
The court is cognizant of the Department’s concern that to allow the
Petitioner’s claim based on an affidavit, and in the absence of a postmarked
envelope, could lead to a flood of claims over the timeliness of filings. The fact
question of timely mailing has been handled by other state and local governmental
agencies, see, e.g., In re Application of the County Collector, 265 Ill. App. 3d at 486-
87 (county clerk); Wickman, 387 Ill. App. 3d at 415-16 (Illinois Property Tax Appeal
Board), without apparent disruption of their operations. Moreover, here the
Petitioner presented unrebutted evidence of timely mailing that was reasonable
and credible in the context of the highly unusual circumstances surrounding
business and governmental operations during the height of the COVID-19
pandemic. With proper evidence of mail handling procedures, and in a less unusual
circumstance, there seems to be little threat to the Department’s administration of
the tax law by accepting that, in this case, the Petitioner has proved that it timely
mailed its 2016 amended return.
11

Conclusion
The Petitioner’s motion for summary judgment is GRANTED and the
Department’s motion for summary judgment is DENIED. Summary judgment is
granted in favor of the Petitioner and against the Department. The Notice of Claim
Denial is reversed, and the matter is remanded to the Department for further
proceedings.
This is a final order subject to appeal under section 3-113 of the
Administrative Review Law, 735 ILCS 5/3-113, and service by email is service
under section 3-113(a), see 35 ILCS 1010/1-90; 86 Ill. Admn. Code § 5000.330. The
Tribunal is a necessary party to this appeal.
